claim: Directed evolution of biomolecules to improve or change their activity is central to many engineering and synthetic biology efforts.
source: The directed evolution of biomolecules to improve or change their activity is central to many engineering and synthetic biology efforts.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Selecting improved variants from gene libraries in living cells requires plasmid expression systems that suffer from variable copy number effects.
source: However, selecting improved variants from gene libraries in living cells requires plasmid expression systems that suffer from variable copy number effects, or the use of complex marker-dependent chromosomal integration strategies.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript and is consistent with established knowledge about plasmid-based systems.

claim: Common yeast centromere containing (CEN) plasmids vary widely in copy number per cell resulting in highly variable expression levels from cell to cell.
source: For example, in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, common yeast centromere containing (CEN) plasmids vary widely in copy number per cell resulting in highly variable expression levels from cell to cell (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 which shows visual evidence of expression variability, and is consistent with cited literature (Yokobayashi et al., 2002; Turner, 2009; Esvelt et al., 2011).

claim: The standard genetic tool of integrating linear DNA into the genome by homologous recombination is too inefficient to insert DNA libraries without multiple steps that rely on dominant selectable markers.
source: To overcome copy number variation in yeast, the standard genetic tool of integrating linear DNA into the genome by homologous recombination is too inefficient to insert DNA libraries without multiple steps that rely on dominant selectable markers for chromosomal integrations (Wingler and Cornish, 2011) or specialized strain backgrounds (DiCarlo et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wingler and Cornish, 2011; DiCarlo et al., 2013a).

claim: Bacterial type II CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has been used successfully in several eukaryotic organisms.
source: Bacterial type II CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has been used successfully in several eukaryotic organisms (Cong et al., 2013; DiCarlo et al., 2013b; Mali et al., 2013a, 2013b; Shalem et al., 2014) but has not been adapted for selection experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 has not been adapted for selection experiments.
source: Bacterial type II CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has been used successfully in several eukaryotic organisms (Cong et al., 2013; DiCarlo et al., 2013b; Mali et al., 2013a, 2013b; Shalem et al., 2014) but has not been adapted for selection experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The Cas9-sgRNA ribonucleoprotein complex precisely generates double-strand breaks (DSBs) in eukaryotic genomes at sites specified by a 20-nucleotide guide sequence.
source: The Cas9-sgRNA ribonucleoprotein complex precisely generates double-strand breaks (DSBs) in eukaryotic genomes at sites specified by a 20-nucleotide guide sequence at the 5′ end of the sgRNA that base pairs with the protospacer DNA sequence preceding a genomic protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) (Sternberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sternberg et al., 2014) and represents established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism.

claim: The presence of the Cas9-produced DSB in genomic DNA can increase the rate of homology-directed repair (HDR) with linear DNA at the DSB locus by several 1000-fold.
source: The presence of the Cas9-produced DSB in genomic DNA can increase the rate of homology-directed repair (HDR) with linear DNA at the DSB locus by several 1000-fold (Storici et al., 2003; DiCarlo et al., 2013b) potentially enabling high-throughput experimental methods.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Storici et al., 2003; DiCarlo et al., 2013b).

claim: Industrial S. cerevisiae strains are more robust compared to laboratory strains.
source: CRISPR-Cas9 could therefore be useful in probing industrial S. cerevisiae strains, which are more robust compared to laboratory strains (Kerr and Service, 2005; Farrell et al., 2006; Rubin, 2008), but for which few genetic tools are available, due to the fact that these strains are often polyploid with low-efficiency mating and sporulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kerr and Service, 2005; Farrell et al., 2006; Rubin, 2008).

claim: Industrial S. cerevisiae strains are often polyploid with low-efficiency mating and sporulation.
source: CRISPR-Cas9 could therefore be useful in probing industrial S. cerevisiae strains, which are more robust compared to laboratory strains (Kerr and Service, 2005; Farrell et al., 2006; Rubin, 2008), but for which few genetic tools are available, due to the fact that these strains are often polyploid with low-efficiency mating and sporulation.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about industrial yeast strains.

claim: A plasmid expressing Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 fused to a nuclear localization signal (Cas9-NLS) efficiently localizes to the nucleus of yeast cells.
source: To optimize the efficiency of HDR in S. cerevisiae mediated by Cas9, we first constructed a plasmid expressing Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 fused to a nuclear localization signal (Cas9-NLS) that efficiently localizes to the nucleus of yeast cells (Figure 2A,B; Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A,B showing the construct and localization data, and citation to prior work (Jinek et al., 2012).

claim: Cas9 expression from the PRNR2 promoter resulted in yeast strains with near wild type fitness.
source: We used an intermediate strength promoter, PRNR2, to express Cas9 for genome targeting experiments, because Cas9 (Cas9-NLS-His8x) expression from the PRNR2 promoter resulted in yeast strains with near wild type fitness whereas Cas9 expressed using strong yeast promoters such as PTDH3 (Lee et al., 2013) reduced yeast fitness relative to wild type cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing growth profiles.

claim: Cas9 expressed using strong yeast promoters such as PTDH3 reduced yeast fitness relative to wild type cells.
source: We used an intermediate strength promoter, PRNR2, to express Cas9 for genome targeting experiments, because Cas9 (Cas9-NLS-His8x) expression from the PRNR2 promoter resulted in yeast strains with near wild type fitness whereas Cas9 expressed using strong yeast promoters such as PTDH3 (Lee et al., 2013) reduced yeast fitness relative to wild type cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing growth profiles, and citation to prior work (Lee et al., 2013).

claim: Cellular levels of sgRNAs correlate with the efficiency of Cas9-mediated genome targeting in mammalian cells.
source: Cellular levels of sgRNAs correlate with the efficiency of Cas9-mediated genome targeting in mammalian cells (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hsu et al., 2013).

claim: The HDV ribozyme would protect the 5′ end of the sgRNA from 5′ exonucleases.
source: We reasoned that the structured ribozyme would protect the 5′ end of the sgRNA from 5′ exonucleases (Houseley and Tollervey, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning and supported by citation to prior work on RNA degradation (Houseley and Tollervey, 2009).

claim: The HDV ribozyme would cleave the RNA immediately 5′ of the ribozyme, removing extraneous RNA sequences.
source: Additionally, the HDV ribozyme would cleave the RNA immediately 5′ of the ribozyme, removing extraneous RNA sequences and allowing flexibility in which promoters can be used, such as tRNAs whose DNA sequences also serve as RNA polymerase III promoters (Marck et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on known properties of HDV ribozyme and supported by citation (Marck et al., 2006).

claim: tRNA sequences used as RNA polymerase III promoters resulted in nearly 100% efficient barcode insertion in diploid yeast at the URA3 locus.
source: With a single sgRNA, we found tRNA sequences used as RNA polymerase III promoters resulted in nearly 100% efficient barcode insertion in diploid yeast at the URA3 locus, resulting in 5-fluororotic acid resistance (Boeke et al., 1984) whereas the non-tRNA promoters were mostly ineffective (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Non-tRNA promoters were mostly ineffective for barcode insertion in diploid yeast at the URA3 locus.
source: With a single sgRNA, we found tRNA sequences used as RNA polymerase III promoters resulted in nearly 100% efficient barcode insertion in diploid yeast at the URA3 locus, resulting in 5-fluororotic acid resistance (Boeke et al., 1984) whereas the non-tRNA promoters were mostly ineffective (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Targeting was highly efficient for every genomic target except LEU2 using tRNATyr as the RNA polymerase III promoter.
source: We also assessed target sequence bias by targeting 11 unlinked yeast genes in diploid S288C yeast cells using tRNATyr as the RNA polymerase III promoter (Supplementary file 2A). We found that targeting was highly efficient for every genomic target except LEU2, which at first was weak but was restored to 100% by selecting a different guide sequence (LEU2-2) as the sgRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 2A.

claim: LEU2 targeting efficiency was restored to 100% by selecting a different guide sequence (LEU2-2).
source: We found that targeting was highly efficient for every genomic target except LEU2, which at first was weak but was restored to 100% by selecting a different guide sequence (LEU2-2) as the sgRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas9/sgRNA system did not result in non-specific genome targeting.
source: We also verified that our CRISPR-Cas9/sgRNA system did not result in non-specific genome targeting by sequencing 9 of the targeted strains (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The tRNAPro promoter enabled highly-efficient barcode insertion into all copies of the URA3 locus in ATCC4124.
source: The non-tRNA promoter previously used in haploid yeast (DiCarlo et al., 2013b), PSNR52, functioned in diploid S288C yeast but failed to result in targeting in the polyploid industrial yeast ATCC4124; in contrast, the tRNAPro promoter enabled highly-efficient barcode insertion into all copies of the URA3 locus in ATCC4124, which we term cis-multiplexing, that is introducing a double-stranded DNA break at a single genomic locus across all chromosomes (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: PSNR52 promoter functioned in diploid S288C yeast but failed to result in targeting in the polyploid industrial yeast ATCC4124.
source: The non-tRNA promoter previously used in haploid yeast (DiCarlo et al., 2013b), PSNR52, functioned in diploid S288C yeast but failed to result in targeting in the polyploid industrial yeast ATCC4124; in contrast, the tRNAPro promoter enabled highly-efficient barcode insertion into all copies of the URA3 locus in ATCC4124, which we term cis-multiplexing, that is introducing a double-stranded DNA break at a single genomic locus across all chromosomes (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1A, and citation to prior work (DiCarlo et al., 2013b).

claim: tRNATyr was inefficient at targeting in ATCC4124 though it was effective in S288C diploid.
source: Notably, tRNATyr was inefficient at targeting in ATCC4124 though it was effective in S288C diploid (Supplementary file 1A), indicating that the choice of tRNA used for the expression of the HDV-sgRNA impacts multiplexing in a strain-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The choice of tRNA used for the expression of the HDV-sgRNA impacts multiplexing in a strain-dependent manner.
source: Notably, tRNATyr was inefficient at targeting in ATCC4124 though it was effective in S288C diploid (Supplementary file 1A), indicating that the choice of tRNA used for the expression of the HDV-sgRNA impacts multiplexing in a strain-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing differential efficiency across strains.

claim: The efficiency of duplex and triplex targeting with two sgRNAs (URA3 and LYP1) or three (URA3, LYP1 and COX10) was 43% and 19%, respectively.
source: The efficiency of duplex and triplex targeting (requiring four and six chromosome cuts, respectively) with two sgRNAs (URA3 and LYP1) or three (URA3, LYP1 and COX10) was 43% and 19%, respectively (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Duplex targeting dropped to 3.5% in cells with sgRNA lacking the 5′ HDV ribozyme.
source: This multiplexed efficiency was dependent on the presence of the HDV ribozyme 5′ of the guide sequence as duplex targeting dropped to 3.5% in cells with sgRNA lacking the 5′ HDV ribozyme (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The presence of the HDV ribozyme increases the intracellular abundance of the sgRNAs by sixfold.
source: We measured the relative cellular abundance of sgRNAs expressed by PSNR52, with and without the 5′ HDV ribozyme, by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and found that the presence of the ribozyme increases the intracellular abundance of the sgRNAs by sixfold (Figure 3E), consistent with the model that sgRNA abundance is rate limiting for CRISPR/Cas targeting (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: sgRNA abundance is rate limiting for CRISPR/Cas targeting.
source: We measured the relative cellular abundance of sgRNAs expressed by PSNR52, with and without the 5′ HDV ribozyme, by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and found that the presence of the ribozyme increases the intracellular abundance of the sgRNAs by sixfold (Figure 3E), consistent with the model that sgRNA abundance is rate limiting for CRISPR/Cas targeting (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hsu et al., 2013) and is consistent with the experimental data.

claim: Haploid trans-multiplexing showed a minimal loss in activity scaling from one to three loci.
source: Haploid trans-multiplexing showed a minimal loss in activity scaling from one to three loci (up to three chromosome cuts) (Figure 3F; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The 5′ tRNA-HDV ribozyme sequence is required for higher order multiplex targeting.
source: These experiments demonstrate that our multiplexed CRISPR/Cas9 system, which we term CRISPRm, is powerful enough to generate multiple marker-free targeted mutations in the yeast genome in a single experiment and that the 5′ tRNA-HDV ribozyme sequence is required for higher order multiplex targeting.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing reduced efficiency without the ribozyme.

claim: The efficiency of Cas9-mediated integration and assembly of three DNA fragments to the URA3 locus was 85% in diploid yeast S288C cells.
source: The efficiency of Cas9-mediated integration and assembly of these three DNA fragments to the correct (URA3) locus was measured by a combination of 5-fluoroorotic acid resistance (5-FOAR) and NatR. We found 85% efficiency of targeting and assembly in both copies of the URA3 locus in diploid yeast S288C cells, and 70% in polyploid ATCC4124 by using the tRNAPro sequence as the sgRNA promoter (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1A), whereas PSNR52-dependent targeting was weaker in S288C cells and non-existent in ATCC4124 cells (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The efficiency of Cas9-mediated integration and assembly of three DNA fragments to the URA3 locus was 70% in polyploid ATCC4124.
source: We found 85% efficiency of targeting and assembly in both copies of the URA3 locus in diploid yeast S288C cells, and 70% in polyploid ATCC4124 by using the tRNAPro sequence as the sgRNA promoter (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1A), whereas PSNR52-dependent targeting was weaker in S288C cells and non-existent in ATCC4124 cells (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: CRISPRm enables the one-step markerless assembly of functional genes from multiple fragments into the S. cerevisiae genome.
source: Thus, CRISPRm enables the one-step markerless assembly of functional genes from multiple fragments into the S. cerevisiae genome, resulting in homozygous insertions into both diploid and polyploid yeast strains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on gene assembly efficiency.

claim: One strain with homozygous cdt-1 N209S/I354N/S360P/T406S/W531L allele showed 2.6-fold increased cellobiose utilization capacity over wild type cdt-1.
source: We then grew the transformants in medium containing cellobiose as the sole carbon source to select for functional cdt-1 alleles and identified one strain with 2.6-fold (homozygous cdt-1 N209S/I354N/S360P/T406S/W531L allele) and one strain with 1.7-fold (homozygous cdt-1 Q45H/F262Y/F533Y allele) increased cellobiose utilization capacity over wild type cdt-1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One strain with homozygous cdt-1 Q45H/F262Y/F533Y allele showed 1.7-fold increased cellobiose utilization capacity over wild type cdt-1.
source: We then grew the transformants in medium containing cellobiose as the sole carbon source to select for functional cdt-1 alleles and identified one strain with 2.6-fold (homozygous cdt-1 N209S/I354N/S360P/T406S/W531L allele) and one strain with 1.7-fold (homozygous cdt-1 Q45H/F262Y/F533Y allele) increased cellobiose utilization capacity over wild type cdt-1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One mutation site (N209S) maps to a site that likely interacts directly with the sugar substrate.
source: Notably, one site maps to a site that likely interacts directly with the sugar substrate (N209S) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural mapping shown in Figure 4B.

claim: One mutation (F262Y) maps to a site immediately adjacent to the nearly universally-conserved PESPR motif in hexose transporters that is involved in transporter dynamics.
source: Whereas two mutations in the second allele (Q45H, F533Y) map to non-conserved regions of the transporters, one (F262Y) maps to a site immediately adjacent to the nearly universally-conserved PESPR motif in hexose transporters that is involved in transporter dynamics (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and citation to prior work (Sun et al., 2012).

claim: The mutation from phenylalanine to tyrosine results in an expanded motif (PESPRY) that is present in all of the major hexose transporters in S. cerevisiae.
source: Furthermore, the mutation from phenylalanine to tyrosine results in an expanded motif (PESPRY) that is present in all of the major hexose transporters in S. cerevisiae (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence analysis and structural mapping shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The quadruple mutant cdt-1 allele resulted in synergistic cellobiose utilization with 3.9-fold increased growth over strains expressing wild-type cdt-1.
source: We then used CRISPRm to introduce the N209S mutation (nucleotide G626A) in the cdt-1Q45H/F262Y/F533Y diploid yeast background. The quadruple mutant cdt-1 allele resulted in synergistic cellobiose utilization with 3.9-fold increased growth over strains expressing wild-type cdt-1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wild-type cdt-1 integrated into the chromosome was barely able to support cellobiose fermentation.
source: We found that wild-type cdt-1 integrated into the chromosome was barely able to support cellobiose fermentation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fermentation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The cdt-1Q45H/N209S/F262Y/F533Y quadruple mutant expressed from the chromosome resulted in complete fermentation of cellobiose.
source: By contrast, the cdt-1Q45H/N209S/F262Y/F533Y quadruple mutant or the cdt-1N209S/F262Y double-mutant expressed from the chromosome resulted in complete fermentation of cellobiose, comparable to wild-type cdt-1 expressed from a high-copy 2µ plasmid (Figure 4C; Ha et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by fermentation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The cdt-1N209S/F262Y double-mutant expressed from the chromosome resulted in complete fermentation of cellobiose.
source: By contrast, the cdt-1Q45H/N209S/F262Y/F533Y quadruple mutant or the cdt-1N209S/F262Y double-mutant expressed from the chromosome resulted in complete fermentation of cellobiose, comparable to wild-type cdt-1 expressed from a high-copy 2µ plasmid (Figure 4C; Ha et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by fermentation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The rate of cellobiose consumption for wild-type cdt-1 was 0.13 g L−1 hr−1.
source: The rate of cellobiose consumption was 0.13 g L−1 hr−1.
evidence: This is a measurement reported from the fermentation experiment shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The rate of cellobiose consumption for mutant cdt-1 strains was over 2.0 g L−1 hr−1.
source: The rate of cellobiose consumption for both strains was over 2.0 g L−1 hr−1.
evidence: This is a measurement reported from the fermentation experiment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CRISPRm can be used to quickly generate markerless loss-of-function alleles, heterologous insertion alleles, allele swaps and engineer proteins in yeast.
source: We have demonstrated that CRISPRm can be used to quickly generate markerless loss-of-function alleles, heterologous insertion alleles, allele swaps and engineer proteins in yeast by in vivo selections for greatly improved metabolic activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental results presented.

claim: The mutations in CDT-1 may improve protein function.
source: Although we selected for improved protein function, as suggested by the location of the mutations in CDT-1 (Figure 4B), it is also possible that selection enriched for sequences that confer improved mRNA stability or translation efficiency, due to the fact that the selection was carried out in vivo.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural location of mutations and the nature of the selection.

claim: Selection may have enriched for sequences that confer improved mRNA stability or translation efficiency.
source: Although we selected for improved protein function, as suggested by the location of the mutations in CDT-1 (Figure 4B), it is also possible that selection enriched for sequences that confer improved mRNA stability or translation efficiency, due to the fact that the selection was carried out in vivo.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations for the observed improvements.

claim: CRISPRm could be used to integrate DNA libraries to interrogate cis-regulatory elements such as transcription promoters, 5′- and 3′-untranslated regions (5′-UTRs and 3′-UTRs) in mRNAs, or riboswitches.
source: CRISPRm could be used to integrate DNA libraries to interrogate cis-regulatory elements such as transcription promoters, 5′- and 3′-untranslated regions (5′-UTRs and 3′-UTRs) in mRNAs, or riboswitches.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: CRISPRm enables near quantitative integration of DNA libraries.
source: CRISPRm enables these types of experiments because it allows for near quantitative integration of DNA libraries, which can be a single fragment or complex assemblies of multiple fragments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing high efficiency integration.

claim: The ability to use chromosomally-integrated DNA libraries removes a key limitation in in vivo selection experiments by eliminating biomolecule expression variation due to variable plasmid copy numbers.
source: The ability to use chromosomally-integrated DNA libraries removes a key limitation in in vivo selection experiments by eliminating biomolecule expression variation due to variable plasmid copy numbers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the demonstrated capabilities and the known problem of plasmid copy number variation.

claim: 2–3 mutations per kilobase were observed in the selected transporter genes.
source: Although we used a relatively small library size in the present experiments, even in this small library we observed impressive gains in transporter function. We observed 2–3 mutations per kilobase in the selected transporter genes, resulting in 3–5 amino acid substitutions per transporter.
evidence: This is a measurement from the sequencing of selected mutants.

claim: The selected transporter genes had 3–5 amino acid substitutions per transporter.
source: We observed 2–3 mutations per kilobase in the selected transporter genes, resulting in 3–5 amino acid substitutions per transporter.
evidence: This is a measurement from the sequencing of selected mutants.

claim: Library sizes introduced by CRISPRm should be scalable to the limits of transformation efficiency, to 107 or larger.
source: Library sizes introduced by CRISPRm should be scalable to the limits of transformation efficiency, to 107 or larger (Kawai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about scalability based on known transformation efficiency limits and citation to prior work (Kawai et al., 2010).

claim: CRISPRm should enable multiple rounds of selection for directed evolution experiments.
source: CRISPRm should also enable multiple rounds of selection for directed evolution experiments.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: CRISPRm should be adaptable to screens that rely on sorting large populations of cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting.
source: CRISPRm should also be adaptable to screens that rely on sorting large populations of cells, that is by fluorescence-activated cell sorting.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: CRISPRm could improve the discovery of human therapeutics by yeast display.
source: We envision that CRISPRm could improve the discovery of human therapeutics by yeast display (Krugel et al., 1988), and could be used to map the importance of protein–protein interactions (Ovchinnikov et al., 2014) via multiplexed library insertion.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications with citations to relevant prior work (Krugel et al., 1988; Ovchinnikov et al., 2014).

claim: CRISPRm could be used to map the importance of protein–protein interactions via multiplexed library insertion.
source: We envision that CRISPRm could improve the discovery of human therapeutics by yeast display (Krugel et al., 1988), and could be used to map the importance of protein–protein interactions (Ovchinnikov et al., 2014) via multiplexed library insertion.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications with citation to relevant prior work (Ovchinnikov et al., 2014).

claim: It was necessary to modify the sgRNA design by including a 5′ HDV ribozyme to achieve high efficiency multiplexing with CRISPRm.
source: To achieve high efficiency multiplexing with CRISPRm, we found it was necessary to modify the sgRNA design by including a 5′ HDV ribozyme, and to assay multiple RNA polymerase III promoters for a given strain background.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing efficiency with and without the ribozyme.

claim: It was necessary to assay multiple RNA polymerase III promoters for a given strain background to achieve high efficiency multiplexing with CRISPRm.
source: To achieve high efficiency multiplexing with CRISPRm, we found it was necessary to modify the sgRNA design by including a 5′ HDV ribozyme, and to assay multiple RNA polymerase III promoters for a given strain background.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing strain-dependent promoter efficiency.

claim: CRISPRm can be used directly in non-model fungal hosts with few modifications.
source: The ease of discovering tRNAs in any genome and the universality of the sgRNA construct means that, with few modifications, CRISPRm can be used directly in non-model fungal hosts, such as pathogens or organisms used in the biotechnology industry.
evidence: This is speculation about applicability to other organisms based on the modular design and universal components.

claim: Industrial S. cerevisiae strains produce much higher yields of desired biofuel or renewable chemical end products than laboratory strains.
source: For example, industrial S. cerevisiae strains are more stress tolerant and produce much higher yields of desired biofuel or renewable chemical end products than laboratory strains (Kerr and Service, 2005; Farrell et al., 2006; Rubin, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kerr and Service, 2005; Farrell et al., 2006; Rubin, 2008).

claim: Linking genotypes of industrial yeasts to their phenotypes remains difficult.
source: However, linking genotypes of industrial yeasts to their phenotypes remains difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: CRISPRm should serve as a rapid and high throughput means for connecting the genotypes of organisms to their phenotypes.
source: CRISPRm should serve as a rapid and high throughput means for connecting the genotypes of these organisms to their phenotypes, that is for generating marker-free barcoded alleles for large-scale pooled fitness studies of loss-of-function mutants in these organisms (Giaever et al., 2002).
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications with citation to relevant prior work (Giaever et al., 2002).

claim: CRISPRm may be applicable to interrogating mammalian cells if the levels of HDR are sufficiently high.
source: In the future, CRISPRm may also be applicable to interrogating mammalian cells, if the levels of HDR are sufficiently high.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications with a conditional statement.

claim: The ability to use CRISPRm for multiplexed targeting paves the way for applying directed evolution to cellular pathways and genetic circuits.
source: Finally, the ability to use CRISPRm for multiplexed targeting paves the way for applying directed evolution to cellular pathways and genetic circuits for higher order synthetic biology applications in any host strain.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: Cas9 requires at least 12 perfect base pair matches within the guide-target sequence.
source: Cas9 requires at least 12 perfect base pair matches within the guide-target sequence (Hsu et al., 2013) so it is highly unlikely that the URA3 and LYP1 guide sequences directed Cas9 to any of these potential protospacers that lie within variant sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hsu et al., 2013).

claim: It is highly unlikely that the URA3 and LYP1 guide sequences directed Cas9 to any of the potential protospacers that lie within variant sites.
source: Cas9 requires at least 12 perfect base pair matches within the guide-target sequence (Hsu et al., 2013) so it is highly unlikely that the URA3 and LYP1 guide sequences directed Cas9 to any of these potential protospacers that lie within variant sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data analysis and known Cas9 targeting requirements.

claim: The mutations identified in the genomes of URA3- and LYP1-targeted strains likely arose as natural variants during the course of the experiment.
source: These mutations likely arose as natural variants during the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis showing poor matches between guide sequences and variant sites.

claim: The variants identified in the genomes of URA3- and LYP1-targeted strains are unlikely the result of off-target Cas9 modifications.
source: Since our guide sequences are expected to have a better match to 13% or more of all Cas9 target sequences (∼126,000 or more sites) than to the best matching Cas9 target sequence with a nearby variant, and the number of nucleotide matches in end-to-end alignments is at most 10, we argue that the variants identified in the genomes of URA3- and LYP1-targeted strains are unlikely the result of off-target Cas9 modifications.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on computational analysis of potential off-target sites.

claim: The variability in the relative expression of two fluorescent proteins is reduced by moving from two plasmids to one.
source: The variability in the relative expression of the two fluorescent proteins is reduced by moving from two plasmids to one, and the variability in total expression is reduced by moving to the genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from visual inspection of Figure 1 comparing panels A and B.

claim: The variability in total expression is reduced by moving to the genome.
source: The variability in the relative expression of the two fluorescent proteins is reduced by moving from two plasmids to one, and the variability in total expression is reduced by moving to the genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from visual inspection of Figure 1 comparing plasmid-based (A, B) to genome-integrated (C, D) expression.

claim: The difference between integrating into one or two loci in the genome is minimal.
source: The difference between integrating into one or two loci in the genome is minimal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from visual inspection of Figure 1 comparing panels C and D.

claim: CRISPRm selected an improved cellobiose utilization pathway in diploid yeast in a single round of mutagenesis and selection.
source: With this Multiplex CRISPR (CRISPRm) system, we selected an improved cellobiose utilization pathway in diploid yeast in a single round of mutagenesis and selection, which increased cellobiose fermentation rates by over 10-fold.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: CRISPRm increased cellobiose fermentation rates by over 10-fold.
source: With this Multiplex CRISPR (CRISPRm) system, we selected an improved cellobiose utilization pathway in diploid yeast in a single round of mutagenesis and selection, which increased cellobiose fermentation rates by over 10-fold.
evidence: This is based on the fermentation data comparing wild-type and mutant strains (rate increased from 0.13 to over 2.0 g L−1 hr−1, which is over 15-fold).

claim: Mutations recovered in the best cellodextrin transporters reveal synergy between substrate binding and transporter dynamics.
source: Mutations recovered in the best cellodextrin transporters reveal synergy between substrate binding and transporter dynamics, and demonstrate the power of CRISPRm to accelerate selection experiments and discoveries of the molecular determinants that enhance biomolecule function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural location of mutations and the synergistic effect observed when combining mutations.

claim: Yeast strain ATCC4124 is an industrial polyploid yeast isolated from a molasses distillery.
source: Yeast strain ATCC4124 is an industrial polyploid yeast isolated from a molasses distillery, and was obtained from ATCC (American Type Culture Collection, Manassas, VA).
evidence: This is factual information about the strain source.

claim: The cellodextrin utilization pathway from Neurospora crassa is comprised of the cellodextrin transporter (cdt-1) and an intracellular β-glucosidase (gh1-1).
source: Finally, we tested whether CRISPRm could be used for in vivo selections of improved protein function. We targeted a cellodextrin utilization pathway from the cellulolytic fungus Neurospora crassa, comprised of the cellodextrin transporter (cdt-1) and an intracellular β-glucosidase (gh1-1), to assemble in vivo in diploid S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is factual information about the pathway components.

claim: The combination of cdt-1 and gh1-1 genes results in yeast cells capable of consuming the disaccharide cellobiose.
source: In combination, these two genes result in yeast cells capable of consuming the disaccharide cellobiose, which could be used to improve biofuel production (Galazka et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Galazka et al., 2010) and is demonstrated by the experimental results.
